```{=html}
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The idea in one table: five scales, five sets of decisions</p>
<table class="lx-mini-table">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Scale</th><th scope="col">Who decides</th><th scope="col">What they decide</th><th scope="col">What a model needs</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>S0 Device and plant</td><td>The owner of a home or plant</td><td>What to install at one site, and how to run it hour by hour</td><td>Device ratings, efficiencies, one meter</td></tr>
<tr><td>S1 Microgrid and community</td><td>A campus owner or a rural co-op</td><td>Size, and which loads stay on when it islands</td><td>A small network that can run alone</td></tr>
<tr><td>S2 Regional bulk grid</td><td>A grid operator, overseen by regulators</td><td>Which plants run, reserves, lines, connections</td><td>Power flow, frequency, inertia</td></tr>
<tr><td>S3 City and region</td><td>A city or county</td><td>Codes, heat, transit, land, feeder upgrades</td><td>Feeders, heat networks, links between sectors</td></tr>
<tr><td>S4 Nation</td><td>A national government and regulators</td><td>Targets, instruments, infrastructure, trade</td><td>Regional energy balances, main corridors</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>A U.S. home draws about 1.2 kW on average; the Southwest Power Pool peaked at 54.4 GW in 2025; the Lower 48 states' record hour needed 759 GW (29 July 2025). Signals and limits pass down the scales; profiles and needs pass up.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you work through this step by step: a zoom through five scenes, five sorts and one question about a campus.</p>
```

## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="f1-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>A scale</dt><dd>A level of the system with its own decision makers, decisions and physics; not just a size on the map. A <span class="lx-term" data-term="microgrid">microgrid</span> (S1) can even <span class="lx-term" data-term="islanding">island</span>.</dd>
<dt>Who decides</dt><dd>An owner (S0), a campus or co-op (S1), a grid operator (S2), a city (S3), a nation (S4).</dd>
<dt>Between scales</dt><dd>Prices, tariffs, limits and targets pass down; load profiles, flexibility and needs pass up.</dd>
<dt>Local optimum</dt><dd>The best plan for one scale, a <span class="lx-term" data-term="local-optimum">local optimum</span>, holds only inside its boundary; a limit from the scale above can change it.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Real organisations straddle scales</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

The five scales are a lens for questions, not an organisation chart.

- **A co-op can sit on two scales.** It can own a campus microgrid (S1) and buy power on the regional grid (S2).
- **One site can matter to a whole grid.** A large factory or data-center campus is one site (S0), yet large enough to change regional planning (S2): Analyst lesson A6 (upcoming).
- **One question can span two scales.** Where new solar goes is a city question (land, S3) and a grid question (connection, S2).
- **Regulators reach across.** One regulator can oversee a utility's grid (S2) and the tariffs its city customers pay (S3): Analyst lesson A4 (upcoming).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Linking models across scales</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

A model of one scale takes the arrows from other scales as **parameters**: given data, not decisions. For example, a campus model keeps its export to the feeder under the limit passed down from the grid:

$$
x_t \;\le\; \bar{X} \quad \text{for every hour } t
$$

with $x_t$ the campus's export in hour $t$ (MW) and $\bar{X}$ the feeder's export limit (MW). Three ways to link scales:

- **One way.** Fix the other scale's numbers as data. Simple, but blind to feedback.
- **Back and forth.** Run two models in turn, passing results until they agree (soft-linking).
- **One model.** Put both scales in one optimization. Consistent, but larger and slower.

Modeler lesson M5 (upcoming) adds the feeder's limit to a campus design; capstone C1 (upcoming) asks who pays.


## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<p class="lx-lede">Practice, about 10 minutes: three myths, then six situations to place on the ladder.</p>
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="f1-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="size" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A scale is just a size on the map.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A scale is set by who decides what and which physics a model needs: Prairie City and the Plains Grid cover the same land.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="local" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The cheapest plan for one campus is also the best plan for the grid it sits on.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A local optimum holds only inside its boundary; the grid weighs everyone's costs and limits, and the two answers can differ.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="homes" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “One household's choices are too small to matter at the national scale.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. One home is small, but millions of homes' profiles add up to the demand that grids and nations plan for: needs pass up the ladder.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="f1">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="island" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A rural co-op decides which loads stay on when its microgrid runs on its own in an outage. Which scale?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">S0 Device and plant</li><li data-value="b">S1 Microgrid and community</li><li data-value="c">S2 Regional grid</li><li data-value="d">S3 City and region</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>S1: load priorities when a microgrid islands are the microgrid's own decision.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="reserve" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">An operator calls on reserves after a large plant trips. Which scale?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">S0 Device and plant</li><li data-value="b">S1 Microgrid and community</li><li data-value="c">S2 Regional grid</li><li data-value="d">S4 Nation</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>S2: reserves keep a whole synchronous grid in balance (lesson 3).</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="code" data-answer="d">
<p class="lx-qtext">A county requires new homes to be wired for heat pumps and EV chargers. Which scale?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">S0 Device and plant</li><li data-value="b">S2 Regional grid</li><li data-value="c">S4 Nation</li><li data-value="d">S3 City and region</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>S3: building codes are a city or county decision, and they shape demand for years.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="stocks" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">A ministry decides how many days of oil imports to keep in emergency storage. Which scale?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">S4 Nation</li><li data-value="b">S3 City and region</li><li data-value="c">S2 Regional grid</li><li data-value="d">S1 Microgrid and community</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>S4: emergency fuel stocks are a national security decision.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="physics" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">Which physics does a regional grid model need that a one-home model does not?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">A battery's state of charge</li><li data-value="b">Power flow on lines and the grid's frequency</li><li data-value="c">The efficiency of a heat pump</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Power flow and frequency: a regional grid is one synchronous network. A home model needs its devices, not the network.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="arrow" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">Which of these travels down the ladder, from a larger scale to a smaller one?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">A home's hourly load</li><li data-value="b">A city's demand forecast</li><li data-value="c">A tariff</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>A tariff: prices, tariffs, limits and targets pass down; loads, forecasts and needs pass up.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>In the United States, the day-to-day balance of each region's grid is run by a balancing authority, usually a utility or a regional transmission organization; cities and states shape demand and siting, and national rules set the frame.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-sources">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Sources and further reading</p>
<ul>
<li>EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/delivery-to-consumers.php">Electricity explained: How electricity is delivered to consumers</a>: balancing authorities manage the day-to-day operation of the grid in their regions. Read 3 November 2026.</li>
<li>EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=97&amp;t=3">Frequently Asked Questions: How much electricity does an American home use?</a> 2022 data.</li>
<li>EIA (2025). <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=65864">U.S. electricity peak demand set new records twice in July</a>. Today in Energy, 5 August 2025.</li>
<li>EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/">Hourly Electric Grid Monitor</a> (Form EIA-930): the Southwest Power Pool's 2025 demand.</li>
</ul>
```
